title: What Is Frontend Development?
description: Understand what frontend engineers actually build, how frontend differs from design and backend work, and why HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are the starting point.

title: How the Web Works
description: Build the core mental model of the web: a browser sends a request to a server, the server sends back a response, and the browser uses that response to continue building the experience.

title: What Happens When You Click a Link?
description: Follow a webpage request from a user's click through DNS, the server response, and the browser's first rendering steps.

title: Browser, Server, and Client
description: Understand the different jobs of the browser and server, why the browser is called the client, and which responsibilities belong on each side of a web application.

title: How Forge Works
description: Learn how Forge's Learn, Practice, and Grow loop turns lessons into active skill-building, and understand what to do after you finish a lesson.

title: Meet Your Browser DevTools
description: Get comfortable with browser DevTools and learn what the Elements, Console, Network, and Sources panels are for before using them to debug real problems.

title: Inspecting HTML with Elements
description: Use the Elements panel to inspect the live DOM, experiment with HTML and CSS changes, and learn the difference between temporary browser edits and changes to your actual source code.

title: Understanding the Console
description: Learn how the browser Console runs JavaScript, shows logs and warnings, and exposes runtime errors that help you investigate what your code is actually doing.

title: Understanding Network Requests
description: Learn how to use the Network panel to see what a webpage requests, what comes back, whether a request succeeded, and how network evidence helps explain frontend problems.

title: Your First Debugging Exercise
description: Put Elements and Console together in a guided debugging drill: inspect the page, identify evidence, explain the cause, and make the smallest fix instead of guessing.

title: HTML: The Structure of the Web
description: Understand HTML as the semantic structure of a webpage and learn how the browser turns a document into a meaningful tree of elements.

title: Elements, Tags, and Attributes
description: Learn how HTML elements are written, how opening and closing tags create structure, and how attributes provide additional information or configuration.

title: Headings, Paragraphs, and Text
description: Practice using HTML headings and paragraphs to create a clear document structure that communicates hierarchy to both people and the browser.

title: Links, Images, and Paths
description: Practice using anchors and images correctly, understand how href and src point to resources, and learn how relative and absolute paths are resolved by the browser.

title: Lists and Tables
description: Practice using HTML lists to represent ordered or unordered collections and tables to represent genuine tabular data.

title: Forms and User Input
description: Build forms that collect user input using labels, inputs, and a submit action, and learn why associating labels with controls is essential for usable HTML.

title: Semantic HTML
description: Learn how semantic HTML elements communicate the role of page regions and content, then refactor generic markup into meaningful structure that is easier to navigate, maintain, and understand.

title: HTML Challenge: Build a Real Page
description: Bring the HTML module together by building a complete page that uses headings, text, links, images, lists, forms, and semantic structure in one coherent document.

title: What Is CSS?
description: Understand CSS as a rule-based styling language, learn the anatomy of a CSS rule, and build the mental model that styles are matched to elements and then resolved.

title: Selectors and Specificity
description: Learn how CSS identifies elements with type, class, ID, attribute, and descendant selectors, then understand why conflicting rules do not all have equal priority.

title: The Cascade and Inheritance
description: Understand how the CSS cascade resolves competing declarations, how inherited properties flow from parent to child, and why !important should not be your first response to a styling conflict.

title: The CSS Box Model
description: Understand how every HTML element becomes a box made of content, padding, border, and margin, and learn how the browser calculates the space that element occupies.

title: Spacing, Sizing, and Layout
description: Turn the box model into practical layout skills by controlling width, height, spacing, and gaps while learning to distinguish element size from the space around it.

title: Typography and Text
description: Learn how CSS controls typography, including font family, size, weight, line height, alignment, and readable text width.

title: Colors, Backgrounds, and Borders
description: Learn how CSS controls foreground and background colors, borders, rounded corners, and simple visual surfaces while keeping contrast and content accessibility in mind.

title: Display and Normal Flow
description: Understand how block and inline elements participate in normal document flow, how the display property changes that behavior, and why layout bugs often begin with misunderstanding the flow.

title: Flexbox Fundamentals
description: Learn how Flexbox arranges elements along a main axis and cross axis, and use it to build practical one-dimensional layouts with predictable alignment and spacing.

title: CSS Grid Fundamentals
description: Learn CSS Grid as a two-dimensional layout system, define rows and columns with tracks, control spacing with gaps, and place content into a predictable grid.

title: Responsive Design and Media Queries
description: Learn how responsive layouts adapt to different viewport sizes using flexible sizing, media queries, and mobile-first CSS.

title: CSS Challenge: Build a Responsive Interface
description: Bring the CSS module together by transforming a structured HTML page into a polished, responsive interface using the cascade, box model, typography, colors, Flexbox, Grid, and responsive design.

title: JavaScript and the Browser
description: Understand what JavaScript actually does in the browser, how it responds to events, and how it changes the live page through the DOM.

title: Variables and Values
description: Learn how let and const give JavaScript names for values, how reassignment works, and why choosing the right declaration makes code easier to reason about.

title: Data Types and Operators
description: Learn the core JavaScript data types and the operators used to calculate, compare, and combine values, with special attention to strict equality and type coercion.

title: Conditions and Decisions
description: Use if, else if, else, and switch to make JavaScript choose what to do based on conditions.

title: Loops and Repetition
description: Practice repeating work with for and while loops, control iteration safely, and avoid the classic off-by-one and infinite-loop mistakes.

title: Functions
description: Learn how functions package reusable logic, accept inputs through parameters, and produce results through return values.

title: Arrays
description: Learn how arrays store ordered collections of values and use push, map, and filter to add, transform, and select data.

title: Objects
description: Learn how JavaScript objects model real-world entities with named properties, and practice reading and updating data with dot and bracket notation.

title: JavaScript Mini Project
description: Build a small working learner-progress application that combines variables, conditionals, loops, functions, arrays, and objects into one coherent JavaScript program.

title: Understanding Browser Rendering
description: Build a clear mental model of how the browser turns HTML and CSS into the pixels you see, from parsing to layout to painting.

title: Reading JavaScript Errors
description: Learn to read JavaScript error types, messages, and stack traces so errors become useful clues instead of scary red walls of text.

title: Console Debugging
description: Use console.log, console.table, and breakpoints to inspect program state at the moment something goes wrong.

title: Debugging DOM Problems
description: Diagnose and fix common DOM failures caused by incorrect selectors, missing elements, and JavaScript running before the DOM is ready.

title: Debug Challenge: Fix the Broken Page
description: Apply DevTools, console inspection, JavaScript debugging, and DOM diagnosis together to find and fix several problems in a deliberately broken page.

title: Advanced Flexbox
description: Go beyond basic Flexbox alignment by controlling wrapping, ordering, and how flex items grow, shrink, and calculate their starting sizes.

title: Advanced CSS Grid
description: Go beyond basic Grid by controlling implicit tracks, auto-placement, flexible minimum and maximum sizes with minmax(), and responsive columns with auto-fit and auto-fill.

title: Positioning and Layering
description: Practice relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky positioning together with z-index to control where elements sit and how they stack.

title: Transitions and Animations
description: Learn how CSS transitions and keyframe animations create motion, control timing and easing, and communicate state changes without turning every interaction into visual chaos.

title: CSS Architecture
description: Learn how naming conventions, file organization, and utility versus component styles keep CSS maintainable as an interface grows.

title: Design Tokens and Design Systems
description: Understand how shared design tokens centralize colors, spacing, typography, and other visual decisions so interfaces remain consistent and easier to change.

title: Advanced Responsive Design
description: Build a production-style responsive interface that combines advanced Flexbox, Grid, positioning, design tokens, and responsive constraints into one coherent system.

title: Scope and Hoisting
description: Understand where JavaScript variables are visible and why declarations behave differently depending on whether you use var, let, or const.

title: Closures
description: Understand how functions can remember variables from the scope where they were created, and use that behavior to build private state and reusable behavior.

title: The this Keyword
description: Learn why this is determined by how a regular function is called, how method calls differ from plain function calls and arrow functions, and how to avoid losing the intended this context in callbacks.

title: Destructuring and Spread
description: Practice destructuring values from arrays and objects and using spread syntax to expand or copy data concisely in modern JavaScript.

title: Array Methods
description: Use map, filter, reduce, and find to transform, select, aggregate, and locate data declaratively instead of rebuilding every operation with manual loops.

title: Modules and Imports
description: Practice using ES modules to split JavaScript into reusable files with explicit imports and exports, and learn to diagnose default-versus-named export mistakes.

title: Promises
description: Understand how Promises represent future asynchronous results, work with pending, fulfilled, and rejected states, and chain asynchronous operations with then and catch.

title: Async and Await
description: Use async functions and await to write Promise-based asynchronous code in a readable, sequential style while preserving the underlying Promise model.

title: Error Handling
description: Practice handling failures in synchronous and asynchronous JavaScript with try/catch and Promise catch, while making sure error handling provides useful recovery or user-facing feedback.

title: Modern JavaScript Challenge
description: Build a small realistic JavaScript feature that combines closures, array methods, ES modules, async/await, and deliberate error handling into one coherent application.

title: Why Version Control Exists
description: Understand why developers use version control to track change history, collaborate safely, roll back mistakes, and work on parallel changes through branches.

title: Git Fundamentals
description: Practice the core local Git workflow by initializing a repository, inspecting changes, staging files, creating meaningful commits, and reading project history.

title: Branches
description: Practice creating, switching between, and understanding Git branches so features can be developed independently before being integrated into the main line.

title: Pull Requests
description: Follow a complete pull request workflow: push a feature branch, open a pull request with a clear description, review the proposed change, respond to feedback, and prepare the branch for integration.

title: Merge Conflicts
description: Learn to read, diagnose, and resolve Git merge conflicts by understanding what both branches intended instead of blindly accepting one side.

title: Professional Git Workflow
description: Combine small focused commits, descriptive messages, feature branches, and reviewed pull requests into a repeatable Git workflow suitable for day-to-day frontend development.

title: What Is an API?
description: Understand APIs as defined contracts between software systems, and learn to read an API's endpoints, parameters, request/response shapes, and documented behavior instead of treating 'the API' as a mysterious black box.

title: HTTP Requests and Responses
description: Understand the structure of HTTP requests and responses, including methods, paths, headers, bodies, and status codes, so you can reason about network communication before using Fetch.

title: JSON
description: Understand JSON as a text format for structured data exchange and practice converting between JSON text and JavaScript values with JSON.parse and JSON.stringify.

title: HTTP Status Codes
description: Learn to read HTTP status codes as meaningful signals about the outcome of a request, with emphasis on the 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, and 5xx response classes.

title: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
description: Understand the intended semantics of the main HTTP methods and practice choosing the appropriate method for reading, creating, replacing, partially updating, and deleting resources.

title: Loading, Error, and Empty States
description: Design and implement explicit loading, error, and empty states so data-driven interfaces remain understandable when data is delayed, unavailable, or simply absent.

title: Working with Fetch
description: Use fetch() to make HTTP requests from JavaScript, inspect the response, handle JSON data, and deliberately handle HTTP failures instead of assuming a rejected Promise means every failed HTTP status.

title: API Integration Project
description: Build a working frontend feature that consumes a real API and handles loading, success, empty, and error states without hardcoding an ideal response shape.

title: Why React?
description: Understand the problem React solves: describing interfaces as reusable components whose rendered output changes when application state changes, instead of manually coordinating DOM updates throughout the application.

title: JSX
description: Learn JSX as the syntax React uses to describe UI, combine markup-like structure with JavaScript expressions, and practice the rules that make JSX different from ordinary HTML.

title: Components
description: Build reusable React components as focused functions that return JSX, and learn to break a growing interface into smaller pieces instead of putting everything inside one giant component.

title: Props
description: Learn how parent components pass read-only data into child components through props, and practice changing those inputs to see the child render different UI.

title: State
description: Learn how useState gives a React component local changing data, why updating state schedules a re-render, and why directly mutating state does not produce the intended React update.

title: Conditional Rendering
description: Practice choosing between JSX branches with ternaries, logical &&, and early returns so components display the correct UI for their current state.

title: Lists and Keys
description: Practice rendering arrays of data into JSX with map and learn why each rendered item needs a stable key that identifies the item across renders.

title: React Mini Project
description: Build a small React application that combines components, props, state, conditional rendering, and lists into one coherent feature.

title: Events in React
description: Wire browser events to React event handlers, pass functions correctly, and practice updating component state in response to user interactions.

title: Controlled Inputs
description: Learn how React state drives an input's value and how onChange keeps the DOM input and React state synchronized.

title: Forms and Validation
description: Build a controlled React form that validates user input, prevents invalid submission, and gives clear feedback at the right time.

title: useEffect
description: Understand when an effect is appropriate, how useEffect synchronizes a component with something outside React, and how dependency arrays determine when the effect is re-run.

title: Side Effects and Cleanup
description: Learn why effects that create subscriptions, timers, or external connections must return cleanup functions so resources are released when dependencies change or the component is removed.

title: Fetching Data in React
description: Combine useEffect and useState to load asynchronous data, represent loading/error/success states, and avoid updating component state after the component is no longer active.

title: React Interaction Challenge
description: Build a complete interactive React feature that combines controlled inputs, effects, and asynchronous data fetching into one coherent user flow.

title: Thinking in Components
description: Learn to look at a UI before coding, decompose it into meaningful component boundaries, and decide where data and responsibilities should live.

title: Props vs State
description: Learn to distinguish parent-provided props from component-owned state, decide which values belong in each, and use ownership to make React data flow predictable.

title: Lifting State Up
description: Learn how to move shared state to the closest common ancestor so sibling components can stay synchronized through props and callbacks.

title: Composition
description: Learn to build flexible React components by composing smaller components through children and other props, rather than creating rigid components packed with special-case branches.

title: Reusable UI Patterns
description: Practice extracting repeated UI into reusable, parameterized components such as cards, modals, and list items, using props and composition instead of copy-pasting similar implementations.

title: Component Architecture Challenge
description: Refactor or design a small React application by applying the component-architecture patterns from this module: deliberate component boundaries, correct state ownership, lifting shared state, composition, and reusable UI patterns.

title: Why Applications Need Routing
description: Understand why multi-view React applications need real client-side routes, how URLs map to views without a full page reload, and why toggling components with local state is not a substitute for routing.

title: Routes and Navigation
description: Implement client-side routes and navigation so users can move between views without unnecessary full page reloads, using router links and navigation APIs.

title: Dynamic Routes
description: Implement routes with dynamic URL segments such as /lessons/:id, read the captured parameter inside the matched component, and handle cases where the parameter does not correspond to real data.

title: Nested Routes
description: Build nested routes so a shared layout such as navigation or a sidebar stays mounted while child route content changes inside it.

title: Navigation State
description: Read navigation information directly from the router, including the current location and query parameters, and use that information to drive UI without creating unnecessary duplicate local state.

title: Build a Multi-Page React App
description: Build a complete multi-page React application that combines nested routes, dynamic parameters, shared layouts, and meaningful application information architecture.

title: Local State vs Global State
description: Learn to distinguish component-local state from application-wide shared state and make the simplest state-ownership decision before reaching for a global store.

title: When Global State Is Actually Needed
description: Learn to recognize the situations where application-wide shared state is genuinely justified, and avoid globalizing state simply because it might be useful later.

title: Zustand Fundamentals
description: Build a minimal Zustand store with state and actions, subscribe to only the state slices a component needs, and use selectors to avoid unnecessary component updates.

title: Persisted State
description: Learn how to persist selected Zustand store data to browser storage so it survives page reloads, while deciding carefully which state is appropriate to persist.

title: Derived State and Selectors
description: Learn to compute values from existing canonical state instead of storing duplicate computed values, and use selectors to expose exactly the information components need.

title: Designing Application State
description: Learn to design an application's state model before implementing stores by deciding what belongs in local, global, derived, or server-owned state.

title: State Management Project
description: Design and implement a real application state model with clear local/global boundaries, persisted preferences, focused Zustand selectors, and derived values rather than duplicated state.

title: Client-Side Data Flow
description: Learn to trace how server data moves through a client application—from request and response into application state or cache and finally into rendered UI—and identify the source of truth at each stage.

title: Caching and Synchronization
description: Learn how client-side caching reduces redundant network requests and why cached data must be synchronized with the authoritative server source over time.

title: Loading States and Skeletons
description: Build loading and skeleton interfaces that communicate asynchronous progress clearly while keeping layout stable and reducing perceived wait.

title: Retries and Error States
description: Build resilient data-fetching flows that distinguish transient failures from permanent errors, provide clear user-facing recovery, and retry deliberately rather than indefinitely.

title: Data Normalization
description: Learn to represent related application entities in flat, ID-keyed structures so each entity has one canonical copy and updates remain consistent across the interface.

title: Building Resilient Interfaces
description: Apply caching, loading states, retries, error handling, and normalized data together so individual failures remain contained and the interface continues to provide useful functionality.

title: Production Data Project
description: Build a production-style data-driven feature that applies the module's caching, loading/error handling, and normalized-data techniques together.

title: Why We Test
description: Understand why automated tests matter in frontend development: they catch regressions early and document expected behavior as executable specifications.

title: What Makes a Web App Slow?
description: Build a diagnostic mental model for frontend performance by identifying whether slowness comes from network work, JavaScript execution, rendering, asset delivery, or unnecessary application work before choosing an optimization.

title: Rendering and Re-Renders
description: Build a mental model for when React components re-render, what work is repeated, and why unnecessary re-renders can become a performance cost without assuming that every re-render is a problem.

title: Memoization
description: Learn how React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback can prevent unnecessary repeated work when measured performance costs justify them, and recognize when memoization adds complexity without meaningful benefit.

title: Code Splitting and Lazy Loading
description: Learn how to reduce initial JavaScript work by splitting application code into smaller chunks and loading routes or components only when they are needed.

title: Performance Investigation Challenge
description: Diagnose and fix a genuinely slow, semi-realistic application using profiling and the performance techniques learned throughout the module, while explaining the actual root cause rather than optimizing the first suspicious-looking code.

title: Why Architecture Matters
description: Understand why frontend architecture affects how easily a codebase can grow, change, and be understood by new engineers.

title: Scalable Folder Structures
description: Compare common frontend folder-organization strategies and learn how to structure a growing codebase so developers can locate related behavior without excessive searching or dependence on one global file-type hierarchy.

title: Feature-Based Architecture
description: Learn to organize frontend code around product features so components, state, and feature-specific logic stay together, while exposing clear boundaries that prevent features from becoming tightly coupled.

title: Shared Logic vs Page Logic
description: Learn to distinguish genuinely reusable application logic from logic that belongs to one page or feature, so shared code remains intentional and page-specific behavior does not become unnecessarily coupled.

title: Designing Boundaries
description: Learn to design explicit module boundaries by deciding what a module exposes publicly and what remains an internal implementation detail, so dependencies stay intentional and refactoring remains safer.

title: Architecture Tradeoffs
description: Learn to compare architecture decisions by explicitly weighing simplicity, flexibility, performance, and team velocity instead of treating a popular pattern as universally correct.

title: Architecture Review Challenge
description: Review an existing frontend codebase, identify architectural friction, and propose concrete, justified, incremental improvements based on feature ownership, shared logic, module boundaries, and explicit tradeoffs.

title: Custom Hooks
description: Learn how to extract reusable stateful logic from React components into custom hooks, while recognizing when extraction is justified and when a one-off abstraction would add unnecessary complexity.

title: Composition Patterns
description: Learn how React composition patterns let components remain flexible by receiving behavior or UI through children and render functions instead of relying on inheritance-style structures.

title: Compound Components
description: Learn how compound components let a family of related React components share implicit state through a common parent while giving consumers a flexible, readable composition API.

title: Controlled and Uncontrolled Components
description: Learn the distinction between components whose important state is driven by the parent and components that manage their own internal state, and understand when each approach is appropriate.

title: Reusable State Logic
description: Apply the React patterns from this module to separate what data changes from how that data is displayed, making stateful behavior reusable across components without coupling it to one component's JSX.

title: Reading Stack Traces
description: Learn to read a stack trace as a call path leading to an error and use it to locate the likely origin of a bug instead of stopping at the line where the error becomes visible.

title: Finding the Real Source of a Bug
description: Learn to separate the visible symptom of a bug from the place where the incorrect state, data, or assumption actually originated, then trace and fix the root cause.

title: Debugging Async Problems
description: Diagnose asynchronous bugs involving race conditions, unhandled rejections, and stale closures across await boundaries by reproducing the failure, tracing the timing and data flow, and fixing the underlying sequencing or state issue.

title: Debugging State Problems
description: Diagnose React state bugs caused by stale closures, unexpected mutation, and incorrect assumptions about when state updates become visible.

title: Debugging Performance Problems
description: Diagnose frontend performance bugs with profiling evidence instead of guesswork, identify the actual bottleneck, apply a targeted fix, and verify that the user's slow experience improves.

title: The App Is Broken. Now What?
description: Build a calm, repeatable debugging triage process for ambiguous application failures: reproduce the problem, isolate the failing area, form a hypothesis, verify it, fix the cause, and confirm the result.

title: Senior Debugging Challenge
description: Independently diagnose and resolve a complex, multi-layered frontend bug under time pressure by applying the debugging techniques from the entire module and verifying that the true root cause has been addressed.

title: Explaining Technical Tradeoffs
description: Learn to explain architecture and implementation decisions by naming the alternatives considered, the constraints involved, the benefits and costs of each option, and why the chosen approach best fits the situation.

title: Frontend Interview Fundamentals
description: Understand the main types of frontend interview rounds, what each round is designed to evaluate, and why effective preparation must cover fundamentals, coding, system design, communication, and behavioral skills.

title: JavaScript Interview Challenges
description: Practice common JavaScript interview problems involving closures, asynchronous behavior, and array/object manipulation while focusing on the underlying concept rather than memorizing a fixed solution.

title: React Interview Challenges
description: Practice React interview problems involving component design, state and effect reasoning, and performance tradeoffs while developing the habit of clarifying requirements before writing code.

title: Debugging Under Time Pressure
description: Practice a fast, structured debugging process in interview conditions by reproducing a seeded failure, isolating the problem, forming and testing a hypothesis, and narrating the reasoning while fixing the bug.

title: Behavioral and STAR Responses
description: Learn to structure clear, concrete behavioral interview answers using Situation, Task, Action, and Result, with emphasis on one specific engineering story and a measurable outcome.

title: Full Mock Interview
description: Complete a realistic, timed frontend interview that combines technical explanation, tradeoff reasoning, JavaScript and React challenges, debugging, and behavioral storytelling while communication is evaluated alongside correctness.

title: Reading a Real Product Specification
description: Turn a written product specification into an actionable understanding of the application by extracting concrete requirements, constraints, acceptance criteria, dependencies, and open questions before implementation begins.

title: Breaking a Product Into Features
description: Turn a product specification into a scoped, sequenced feature backlog that is small enough to estimate, implement, test, and review incrementally.

title: Planning the Architecture
description: Translate the feature backlog into a high-level frontend architecture by defining data flow, component boundaries, routing, and responsibility before implementation begins.

title: Building the Interface
description: Build the project interface incrementally, moving from static structure to interactive components while keeping each stage visible, testable, and aligned with the architecture and feature backlog.

title: Connecting Data and Interactions
description: Wire the project interface to real state, APIs, and user actions while preserving the component boundaries established during planning and keeping the UI independent from one specific data-source shape.

title: Testing and Debugging
description: Test the integrated project feature against expected behavior, edge cases, and failure states, then use the resulting evidence to identify and fix defects before the feature is considered complete.

title: Performance and Accessibility Review
description: Audit the finished project against measurable performance and accessibility expectations, identify issues systematically, remediate the highest-impact problems, and document the evidence that the final build meets the review standard.

title: Ship It
description: Prepare the completed project for release by verifying the production build, deployment configuration, environment assumptions, and real deployed behavior rather than treating the final commit as the end of the work.

title: Present and Defend Your Project
description: Present the finished project as an engineering case study, explaining the problem, product decisions, architecture, tradeoffs, implementation choices, and what you would improve next.

title: Unit Tests
description: Write focused unit tests for pure functions and logic using Vitest, and learn what makes a test worth keeping.

title: Component Tests
description: Test React components with React Testing Library by rendering them and asserting on what a user would see, not on internal state.

title: Integration Tests
description: Test how several units work together — a form talking to validation logic, a component talking to a mocked API — instead of testing each piece alone.

title: Testing User Behaviour
description: Practice writing tests around real user flows end-to-end within a component tree, combining what you've learned about unit, component, and integration tests.

title: Capstone: Test Suite
description: Write a complete test suite for a small feature, combining unit, component, and integration tests at the level a real code review would expect.

title: Why Accessibility Matters
description: Understand who accessibility is for, why it's a core engineering concern rather than an optional polish step, and what 'inaccessible' actually looks like in real code.

title: Semantic Interfaces
description: Use native HTML elements for their intended purpose so assistive technology gets accurate structure and behavior for free, and learn when ARIA is genuinely needed.

title: Keyboard Navigation
description: Make sure every interactive element in your UI can be reached and operated using only a keyboard, in a logical order.

title: Focus Management
description: Deliberately move keyboard focus for dynamic UI — modals, route changes, toasts — so keyboard and screen reader users aren't left stranded.

title: Labels, Roles, and Accessible Names
description: Give every interactive element and image an accurate accessible name, so assistive technology announces what a control actually does.

title: Capstone: Accessibility Audit
description: Run a full accessibility audit of a real interface, combining automated tooling with a required manual keyboard and screen reader pass, and produce fixes.

title: Capstone: Pattern Workshop
description: Combine custom hooks, composition, compound components, and controlled/uncontrolled design into one reusable component you'd be comfortable publishing for other engineers to use.

title: How to Explain What You Know
description: Learn to communicate technical knowledge clearly under interview conditions — structuring an answer, calibrating depth, and thinking out loud without losing the thread.

title: Error Boundaries
description: Contain rendering errors to a small part of the UI with error boundaries, instead of letting one broken component take down the whole app.

title: Graceful Failure
description: Design interfaces that degrade usefully when something goes wrong — a failed request, a slow connection, a broken third-party script — instead of leaving the user with a blank screen or silent failure.

title: Image and Asset Optimization
description: Learn to reduce the amount of image and static-asset work a browser must download and process by choosing appropriate dimensions, formats, loading strategies, and delivery approaches.

title: Performance Measurement and Budgets
description: Measure real performance with Core Web Vitals and Lighthouse, and set performance budgets so regressions are caught before they ship rather than discovered by users.

title: Why TypeScript?
description: Understand what problem static typing solves that plain JavaScript doesn't, and why catching errors at compile time beats catching them in production.

title: Basic Types
description: Learn TypeScript's primitive and array types, type inference, and the crucial difference between any and unknown.

title: Interfaces and Type Aliases
description: Model the shape of objects with interface and type, and know when each is the idiomatic choice.

title: Typing Functions
description: Type function parameters and return values, including optional parameters and full function type signatures.

title: Union Types and Narrowing
description: Model values that can be one of several types using unions, and safely narrow them with typeof, in, and discriminated unions.

title: Generics Fundamentals
description: Understand why generics exist — writing reusable, type-safe functions and structures — rather than treating them as unexplained syntax.

title: Typing Real-World Data
description: Type a real fetch response and API payload, extending what you learned about APIs earlier in module-2-4 with actual type safety.

title: Capstone: Convert a JS Project to TypeScript
description: Take a small existing JavaScript feature and add types incrementally, mirroring a real onboarding task on a codebase migrating to TypeScript.

title: Why Frontend Security Matters
description: Understand the frontend's real attack surface and why 'the backend handles security' is a dangerous myth.

title: XSS and Input Sanitization
description: Understand reflected, stored, and DOM-based XSS, and why APIs like dangerouslySetInnerHTML are dangerous by default.

title: CSRF and the Same-Origin Policy
description: Understand what CSRF actually exploits, and how the browser's same-origin policy protects against it -- and where it doesn't.

title: CORS in Practice
description: Debug a real CORS error by understanding preflight requests, allowed origins, and allowed headers.

title: Auth Patterns and Token Storage
description: Compare cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage for storing auth tokens, and understand why localStorage-stored JWTs are a common real-world mistake.

title: Capstone: Security Audit of a Frontend App
description: Apply a real security checklist to a provided app, finding and remediating at least one real issue, mirroring lesson-4-4-6's audit structure.

title: Why Meta-Frameworks?
description: Understand SSR vs. CSR vs. SSG vs. ISR, what problem each rendering strategy solves, and when plain client-side React isn't enough.

title: App Router Fundamentals
description: Learn file-based routing, layouts, and nested routes in Next.js's App Router, directly extending module-3-4's routing concepts.

title: Server Components vs. Client Components
description: Understand the actual boundary between Server and Client Components and the common 'why is this breaking' mistakes that happen at it.

title: Data Fetching in Next.js
description: Compare server-side data fetching patterns to the client-side patterns from module-4-2, without re-teaching what you already know.

title: API Routes and Server Actions
description: Build backend-adjacent logic inside the same Next.js project, using both Route Handlers and Server Actions, and know when to reach for each.

title: Rendering Strategy and Performance
